heading: Twenty kingdoms and the forts that outlasted them
body: Rajasthan's history is not the history of one kingdom but of roughly twenty, a patchwork of independent Rajput states that, for most of the last thousand years, never fully unified under a single crown. Who the Rajputs actually were is itself disputed: one theory holds they descended from Central Asian invaders — Shakas, Kushanas, Hunas — who settled and were absorbed into Hindu society; another insists they were native Kshatriya lineages all along; most historians today lean toward a mixed picture, in which local warrior clans, tribal chiefs and absorbed outsiders alike were folded into a shared Rajput identity over centuries. What's not disputed is what they built: an unmatched concentration of hill forts, each the seat of a clan fighting to keep its own patch of desert and scrubland.

Chittorgarh Fort, seat of the Sisodia Rajputs of Mewar from the 8th century to the 16th, is the largest fort complex in the country — a 700-acre citadel on a plateau 150 metres above the plain, holding 65 historic structures including nearly 20 temples. It was besieged three times: by the Delhi Sultan Ala-ud-din Khilji in 1303, by Gujarat's Bahadur Shah in 1533, and finally by the Mughal emperor Akbar, who took it in 1568 — Jahangir handed it back to the Rajputs in 1616. Each siege at Chittorgarh is remembered in Rajput tradition for jauhar, the mass self-immolation of women rather than face capture, a practice that is central to how Mewar tells its own history and impossible to verify in detail from outside sources.

Other Rajput houses took different paths — some, like Amber and later Jaipur, allied with the Mughals through marriage and military service rather than resisting them, and prospered accordingly. That divide, between the states that fought the Mughals and the states that married into them, runs through Rajasthan's architecture as clearly as its politics: it is the difference between a fortress built to withstand a siege and a palace built to host an emperor.
The sites on this map are drawn from both traditions — the forts that were fought over and the courts that negotiated instead.
